tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

The controller is the top layer of our service. It has the requestmapping for /inventory and then we added a new post mapping for our purchase inventory function with "/{skuId}/purchase". This is appended to the request mapping for the full endpoint. 

The purchaseInventory function has one path variable the skuId and a requestbody the InventoryQuantity object with the quantity filed inside. Most of that is right: `@RequestMapping` plus `@PostMapping` joined into the full path, one path variable, the body read into `InventoryQuantity`. Three things to sharpen:

**1. `@Valid` does less than you said.** Three separate steps run before your function, and `@Valid` is only the last of them:

| Step | Who does it | What it checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `@RequestBody` picks a message converter | `Content-Type` is JSON, otherwise `400 Content-Type must be application/json` |
| 2 | `@RequestBody`: Jackson reads the body | body is readable JSON with an int `quantity`, otherwise `400 Invalid request body` |
| 3 | `@Valid` runs Bean Validation | the `@Min(1)` on `quantity`, otherwise `400 quantity must be at least 1` |

Remove `@Valid` and steps 1 and 2 still happen, but `{"quantity": 0}` would get through to the service. Interviewers like this distinction: `@RequestBody` means "turn the body into an object", and `@Valid` means "now check that object's constraints".

**2. A small slip:** the controller calls the **service** (`inventoryService.purchaseInventory`), not the repository. The service then calls the repository. Controller → service → repository, one layer at a time.

**3. Why not `receiveInventory`?** A path variable matches exactly one path segment. `/{skuId}` can match `widget` but never `widget/purchase`, so the only mapping that fits is `/{skuId}/purchase`. One odd case to know: `POST /inventory/purchase` is a *receive* for a SKU named `purchase`, because there `purchase` sits in the `{skuId}` slot.

**Why pass just the `Int`:** you had the what; here's the why. `InventoryQuantity` is a web-layer class. It carries a Bean Validation annotation and exists to match the JSON body. Passing a plain `Int` keeps the service free of web types, so the service could be called from a message queue or a batch job without inventing a fake request body.

Not quite. The answer is **`400`**. Your instinct that the URL gets checked first is correct, but the URL isn't where the "missing" problem lives. Here's another way to see it.

**Spring doesn't know which SKUs exist.** To Spring, `/inventory/missing/purchase` is a perfectly good URL: `{skuId}` matches any text, so `missing` is as valid as `widget`. Routing succeeds. The fact that `missing` isn't in the table is only discovered when the **repository runs a SQL query**, and that happens inside your function body. The URL itself has nothing wrong with it.

To your question: yes, there is a fixed order, and all of it runs before your function:

```
1. Routing          URL + method → purchaseInventory       (a truly bad URL fails here: 404/405)
2. @RequestBody     Content-Type, then Jackson reads JSON  → 400
3. @Valid           @Min(1) on quantity                     → 400   ← {"quantity": 0} stops HERE
4. your function →  service → repository → SQL              → 404   ← "missing" would be found here
```

The request never gets to step 4, so nothing ever asks the database about `missing`.

Think of a bouncer at a club. They check your ID at the door (the body). Whether the bar has run out of your drink (the SKU) only matters once you're inside, and with a bad ID you never get in.

This is also the **cheaper** order: a bad body is rejected without a database round trip. Interviewers may ask "why 400 and not 404?", and "validation runs before the handler, so we never pay for a DB lookup on a malformed request" is a strong answer.

The test that pins this down is [InventoryControllerTest.kt:359](src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt#L359), `POST purchase with an invalid quantity for a missing SKU is a 400`.

**Optional experiment:** temporarily delete `@Valid` from `purchaseInventory` and run that test. The `@Min(1)` check no longer runs, a quantity of `0` reaches the database, and the test fails. That shows you exactly which step was catching it. Then put `@Valid` back.

Does that make sense? If it does, we'll move on to **InventoryService.purchaseInventory**.

### `purchaseInventory`: one branch per outcome

```kotlin
/**
 * Removes quantity from a SKU's stock during a purchase. Returns the remaining InventoryItem on a success.
 * @throws SkuNotFoundException when no sku is found.
 * @throws InsufficientInventoryException if not enough quantity for the purchase.
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException if quantity is less than 1 (a caller bug, so it surfaces as a 500).
 */
fun purchaseInventory(skuId: String, quantity: Int): InventoryItem {
    // Why: @Valid only protects HTTP requests; this also stops direct callers (Can't have a 0 quantity in a purchase and a negative value would add stock.).
    require(quantity >= 1) {"quantity must be at least 1, was $quantity"}
    return when (val purchaseOutcome = inventoryRepository.removeStock(skuId,quantity)){
            is PurchaseResult.Purchased -> purchaseOutcome.item
            PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound -> throw SkuNotFoundException(skuId)
            PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock -> throw InsufficientInventoryException(skuId)
        }
}
```

**What it does:** it checks the argument, asks the repository to buy, and turns the repository's
[`PurchaseResult`](PurchaseResult.kt.md) into what the API needs. On success it returns the item;
for each failure it throws the matching domain exception.

**The `require`, again:** this is the same precondition as
[`receiveInventory`](#receiveinventory-a-precondition-and-a-block-body), and it matters more here.
With `-5`, the repository's `quantity >= -5` is always true and `quantity - (-5)` *adds* 5. The
database `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` wouldn't catch it, because the stock goes up, not down. Only this
line stops a purchase that adds stock. `InventoryServiceTest` checks `0` and `-5`.

**Kotlin (`when` with a subject):** `when (x) { ... }` compares one value, the **subject**, against
each branch in order. It's a much more capable version of Java's `switch`. The branches here use two
kinds of check:

| Branch | Kind | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `is PurchaseResult.Purchased ->` | type check | "is the subject a `Purchased`?" (Java's `instanceof`) |
| `PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound ->` | equality | "is the subject equal to the `SkuNotFound` object?" |

The two `data object`s have exactly one instance each, so an equality check is enough.
`is PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound` would also work. `Purchased` needs `is`, because every successful
purchase creates a new `Purchased`, and there's no single instance to compare against.

**Kotlin (`val` in the subject):** `when (val purchaseOutcome = ...)` calls the repository once,
names the result, and limits that name to the `when`. Outside the braces, `purchaseOutcome` doesn't
exist. The branches need the name, because `.item` is read from it.

**Kotlin (smart cast, with a type):** `purchaseOutcome` has the declared type `PurchaseResult`, and
that interface has no `item`. In the `is PurchaseResult.Purchased` branch, the compiler knows it's a
`Purchased`, so `purchaseOutcome.item` compiles. That's a
[smart cast](InventoryRepository.kt.md#choosing-the-outcome-a-when-without-a-subject), this time
from an `is` check instead of a null check. Think of `Purchased` as a box and `item` as what's inside
it: the service returns what's inside (`InventoryItem`), not the box. Java 16+ equivalent:

```java
if (outcome instanceof PurchaseResult.Purchased p) return p.item();
```

**Kotlin (exhaustive, with no `else`):** there are three branches and no `else`, and it compiles
because `PurchaseResult` is [sealed](PurchaseResult.kt.md#a-sealed-interface). The compiler knows
these are the only three cases, and it checks that each one is handled. That's better than adding an
`else`. If a fourth case were added to `PurchaseResult`, this `when` would stop compiling until
someone decided how the service handles it. With an `else`, the new case would silently fall into
whatever the `else` did.

**Kotlin (`when` is an expression):** the `when` produces a value, and `return` returns it. The
branches have the types `InventoryItem`, `Nothing` and `Nothing`
([`throw` is an expression of type `Nothing`](#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error)), so the
whole `when` has type `InventoryItem`, which matches the return type. The same `Nothing` rule is
what lets `?: throw` produce a non-null result in `getInventory`.

**Watch out: `return` and a line break.** `return` and the start of the `when` have to be on the
same line. In Kotlin, a line break after a bare `return` ends the statement, so this:

```kotlin
return
    when (val purchaseOutcome = ...) { ... }
```

is parsed as `return` with no value, followed by an unreachable `when`. The compiler rejects it,
because the function has to return an `InventoryItem`. Robert ran into this while writing the
function. Java doesn't have this trap, because semicolons, not line breaks, end statements.

**Why the exceptions are thrown here:** the repository reports *what happened*, and the service
decides *what that means*. This follows the same split as
[`getInventory`](#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error). `SkuNotFoundException` is the same
exception `GET /inventory/{skuId}` uses, so the purchase endpoint's `404` comes from the same
handler with the same body.

**KDoc:** one `@throws` for each exception a caller can see, each saying *when*. "Returns the
remaining InventoryItem" says what the `200` body contains: the stock after the purchase, not the
amount bought. Robert changed it from "the new InventoryItem" in review, to match the controller's
KDoc and the contract's "remaining inventory for the SKU".

**Naming:** `purchaseInventory` is the business word. The repository's `removeStock` is the data
word for the same action, the same pairing as `receiveInventory` and `addStock`.

**Kotlin:** `removeStock(skuId,quantity)` with no space after the comma, and `){` with no space,

**Role:** the controller hands over `(skuId, quantity)`. The service asks the repository to do the purchase, then turns the repository's answer into either a return value or an exception. The repository says what happened; the service decides what that means for the API.

[InventoryService.kt:37-51](src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryService.kt#L37-L51)

```kotlin
fun purchaseInventory(skuId: String, quantity: Int): InventoryItem {

    require(quantity >= 1) {"quantity must be at least 1, was $quantity"}
    return when (val purchaseOutcome = inventoryRepository.removeStock(skuId,quantity)){
            is PurchaseResult.Purchased -> purchaseOutcome.item
            PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound -> throw SkuNotFoundException(skuId)
            PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock -> throw InsufficientInventoryException(skuId)
        }

```

Over to you. Explain it in your own words, and try to cover:

1. **`require`**: we just established that `@Valid` already rejects `quantity = 0`. So why is this here too? Your comment says a negative value "would add stock". Walk me through how that happens.
2. **`when (val purchaseOutcome = ...)`**: what does putting the `val` inside the parentheses do?
3. **The branches**: why does the first one say `is PurchaseResult.Purchased`, while the other two have no `is`?
4. **No `else`**: Java's `switch` usually needs a `default`. Why does this compile without an `else`?

`PurchaseResult` is the next file, so for #3 and #4 a rough answer is fine. We'll go deeper there.

The service layer is the core of our code. We have added the purchaseInventory function which is called by the controller layer and calls the repository layer. It requires a skuId string and a quantity int. 
We have added a require section to the function block. This is another check to make sure quantity is at least 1. We have this guard here in case this function is called from somewhere besides the controller level where we have a guard there too with the @Valid annotation.

Our response from the repository is more complicated and can be 1 of 3 things and we assess that by creating a tempoary object (val purchaseOutcome) for the response. So we set up a when condition (if, else if, else in java. Just is then the conditions below in Kotlin) so we can assess what the response from the repository layer is. 
The first is the excpeted 200 outcome. Where we have the returned successful remaining inventory stock in the returned InventoryItem. 
The second is the SkuNotFound object inside the PurchaseResult interface is returned and so we throw the SkuNotFoundException. 
The last case is the InsufficientStock object inside the PurchaseResult interface is returned. Meaning there was not enough stock for the purchase so we throw the InsufficientInventoryException.

That's a solid overview: the extra `require` check for callers that don't come through HTTP, the three outcomes, and which exception each one throws. You skipped a few of the specific questions, so here's what's behind them.

**`when`: closer to `switch` than to if/else.** Kotlin has two forms:
- `when (x) { a -> ...; b -> ... }` **with a subject**, like here, compares one value against each branch. That's Java's `switch`.
- `when { cond1 -> ...; cond2 -> ... }` **without a subject** is the if / else-if chain. You'll see that form in the repository.

Also note the `return when`: in Kotlin, `when` produces a value, so the whole thing can be returned. The first branch produces an `InventoryItem`. The two `throw` branches have type `Nothing`, meaning "never produces a value", so the type of the whole `when` works out to `InventoryItem`.

**The `val` in the parentheses (#2).** You're right that it names the result. Two more details: the repository is called **once**, and the name `purchaseOutcome` exists only inside the `when`'s braces. It's a tightly scoped temporary.

**`is` vs. no `is` (#3).** This is about how many instances each case has:
- `SkuNotFound` and `InsufficientStock` are `data object`s. Exactly one instance of each exists in the whole program, so "is it equal to that object?" is enough.
- `Purchased` is a `data class`. Every successful purchase creates a **new** `Purchased(item)`, so there's no single instance to compare against. You have to ask "is it *of type* `Purchased`?", which is Java's `instanceof`.

And a bonus: `purchaseOutcome` is declared as a `PurchaseResult`, which has no `item` field. Inside the `is Purchased` branch, the compiler knows it's a `Purchased` and lets you read `.item`. That's a **smart cast**. Java 16+ equivalent: `if (outcome instanceof Purchased p) return p.item();`

**No `else` (#4).** `PurchaseResult` is `sealed`, so the compiler knows these three are the only possible cases and confirms you've handled all of them. We'll dig into why that beats an `else` in the next file.

A small wording point: you called the first branch "the 200 outcome". It becomes a 200, but the service doesn't know about HTTP. It just returns an item. The controller and Spring are what turn that into a 200.

---

Any questions on the service?

If not, here's the check question, about the one part you didn't explain:

> Suppose someone deletes the `require` line and calls `purchaseInventory("widget", -5)` directly (no HTTP, so no `@Valid`). `widget` has 10 in stock. Your repository SQL does roughly `SET quantity = quantity - :requested_quantity ... WHERE quantity >= :requested_quantity`. What is `widget`'s stock afterwards, and would the database's `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint stop it?
I think the databases quantity would stop it as -5 is less than 0. If it didnt it would add to the stock and it would then return as 15.

You had the arithmetic right (it ends up at 15), but the `CHECK` would **not** stop it, and that's exactly why the `require` exists. The key is **what** the `CHECK` looks at.

`CHECK (quantity >= 0)` is a rule on the **value stored in the row**, checked after the row is changed. It never sees the request parameter `-5`. Trace it step by step:

| Step | What Postgres evaluates | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WHERE quantity >= :requested_quantity` | `10 >= -5` | true, so the row qualifies |
| `SET quantity = quantity - :requested_quantity` | `10 - (-5)` | `15` |
| `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` on the new row | `15 >= 0` | passes |

Every guard in the database says yes, and the "purchase" silently adds 5 units. The `CHECK` is there to stop stock from going **below zero**, which is the oversell case. A negative purchase moves stock **up**, so it's the one bug the `CHECK` can't catch.

So the layers split the work like this:
- `@Valid` covers HTTP callers.
- `require` covers **every** caller of the service. It's the only thing that stops a negative purchase.
- The `CHECK` is the last line of defense against overselling, whatever the application code does.

This is a strong interview point: "the DB constraint protects the invariant *stock ≥ 0*; it doesn't validate *intent*. A negative purchase satisfies the invariant while being nonsense, so input validation still has to live in the application." `InventoryServiceTest` pins it with `0` and `-5`.

Does that make sense? If it does, next is **PurchaseResult.kt**, which is where the `sealed` question from #4 gets answered.
yes it makes semse. input validation has to live in the application is a good thing to remember.

33	the two queries. The decision (Robert, 2026-09-29) was to have one SQL statement work out the
34	outcome, and one type that carries each outcome separately.

37	- **Throw from the repository.** This would work, but then the repository decides what counts as
38	  an error, which is the service's job (see

41	  can't carry the item, so it would need a separate `item: InventoryItem?` next to it. The compiler

44	### A sealed interface
45

47	/** PurchaseResult is returned by the repository and translated by the service. */
48	sealed interface PurchaseResult {
49	```
50

52	implement. This one has no members at all. It exists only so the three cases share one type, which
53	lets `removeStock` declare a single return type, `PurchaseResult`.

56	`PurchaseResult` must be declared in the same package and the same module (for this project, the
57	`inventory` package inside this Gradle build). No other code can add a fourth case. The compiler
58	therefore knows the complete list, and that is what makes the service's `when` work without an
59	`else` branch (see [exhaustive `when`](InventoryService.kt.md#purchaseinventory-one-branch-per-outcome)).
60	If someone later adds a fourth case here, every `when` over `PurchaseResult` that lacks an `else`
61	stops compiling until it handles the new case. A type change produces a list of every place that
62	needs updating.

65	list can be left out only when they are all in the same file:

87	data class Purchased(val item: InventoryItem) : PurchaseResult
88	```

91	`PurchaseResult.Purchased`, and that is how the repository and the service refer to it. Nesting
92	keeps the three cases grouped under the type they belong to. A nested class in Kotlin is like a
93	`static` nested class in Java: it has no hidden link to an outer object. (In a class, Kotlin's `inner`
94	keyword would add that link. It isn't even allowed inside an interface, since there's no outer instance.)
95	
96	**Kotlin (`data class`):** the same feature as [`InventoryItem`](InventoryItem.kt.md). The
97	generated `equals` is what lets the repository test compare a whole result in one line:
98	`assertEquals(PurchaseResult.Purchased(InventoryItem("widget", 3)), removeStock(...))`.

101	it's an interface, there are no parentheses after the name: there's no constructor to call. Compare
102	with [`: RuntimeException(...)`](error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md#the-whole-class-in-one-line), which
103	extends a class and therefore calls its constructor.

105	**Why it carries an `InventoryItem`:** a successful purchase has data, the remaining stock, and

## Role

Robert wrote this type. It is the answer the [repository's `removeStock`](InventoryRepository.kt.md#removestock-three-outcomes-from-one-statement)

A purchase can end in three ways, and the API answers each one differently:

| Case | Meaning | Service does | Client gets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Purchased(item)` | the SKU had enough stock, and it was deducted | returns `item` | `200` with the remaining stock |
| `SkuNotFound` | there is no row for that SKU | throws `SkuNotFoundException` | `404` |
| `InsufficientStock` | the row exists but holds less than requested | throws `InsufficientInventoryException` | `400` |

This file contains no logic. It only names the three outcomes, so the repository can report what the
SQL found without deciding what that means for HTTP.

## Walkthrough

### Why a new type at all

```kotlin
// Why: We used the sealed interface because we have 3 possible outcomes we need to account for. Not just a success or null so returning InventoryItem? doesn't help us between when we need to throw 404 or 400.
```

**Why:** `addStock` has two outcomes, a row or a refusal, so it returns
[`InventoryItem?`](InventoryRepository.kt.md#findbyskuid-a-nullable-return-type) and uses `null`
for the refusal. A purchase has two different failures. If `removeStock` returned `InventoryItem?`,
a `null` couldn't say which failure happened, and the service would have to go back to the database
to find out. That second query is a race: another request could create or change the SKU between
the two queries. The decision (Robert, 2026-09-29) was to have one SQL statement work out the
outcome, and one type that carries each outcome separately.

Alternatives that were considered:
- **Throw from the repository.** This would work, but then the repository decides what counts as
  an error, which is the service's job (see
  [why throw in the service](InventoryService.kt.md#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error)).
- **An `enum` plus a nullable item.** `enum class Outcome { PURCHASED, NOT_FOUND, INSUFFICIENT }`
  can't carry the item, so it would need a separate `item: InventoryItem?` next to it. The compiler
  couldn't then guarantee that `PURCHASED` always comes with an item.

### A sealed interface

```kotlin
/** PurchaseResult is returned by the repository and translated by the service. */
sealed interface PurchaseResult {
```

**Kotlin (`interface`):** a Kotlin interface works like a Java interface: a type that other classes
implement. This one has no members at all. It exists only so the three cases share one type, which
lets `removeStock` declare a single return type, `PurchaseResult`.

therefore knows the complete list, and that is what makes the service's `when` work without an
`else` branch (see [exhaustive `when`](InventoryService.kt.md#purchaseinventory-one-branch-per-outcome)).

needs updating.

**Java equivalent:** Java 17 has the same feature. The subtypes are listed with `permits`, and the
list can be left out only when they are all in the same file:

```java
public sealed interface PurchaseResult
        permits PurchaseResult.Purchased, PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound, PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock {
    record Purchased(InventoryItem item) implements PurchaseResult {}
    final class SkuNotFound implements PurchaseResult { /* a singleton, by hand */ }
    final class InsufficientStock implements PurchaseResult { /* a singleton, by hand */ }
}
```

Kotlin never uses a `permits` list, and its rule is looser: a subtype can be in any file of the
same package and module, while Java without `permits` allows only the same file.

**Sealed interface or sealed class:** `sealed class PurchaseResult` would also work. An interface
fits better here because the cases share no state or code. A class can extend only one class but
can implement many interfaces, so using an interface keeps that option open.

### The success case: a `data class`

```kotlin
/** The SKU exists and had enough stock. Item holds the remaining stock. */
data class Purchased(val item: InventoryItem) : PurchaseResult
```

`PurchaseResult.Purchased`, and that is how the repository and the service refer to it. Nesting
keeps the three cases grouped under the type they belong to. A nested class in Kotlin is like a
`static` nested class in Java: it has no hidden link to an outer object. (In a class, Kotlin's `inner`
keyword would add that link. It isn't even allowed inside an interface, since there's no outer instance.)

**Kotlin (`data class`):** the same feature as [`InventoryItem`](InventoryItem.kt.md). The
generated `equals` is what lets the repository test compare a whole result in one line:
`assertEquals(PurchaseResult.Purchased(InventoryItem("widget", 3)), removeStock(...))`.

**Kotlin (`: PurchaseResult`):** this declares that `Purchased` implements the interface. Because
it's an interface, there are no parentheses after the name: there's no constructor to call. Compare
with [`: RuntimeException(...)`](error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md#the-whole-class-in-one-line), which

**Why it carries an `InventoryItem`:** a successful purchase has data, the remaining stock, and
the service returns it as the `200` body. The two failures have no data, so they don't need a class

### The failure cases: `data object`

```kotlin

data object SkuNotFound : PurchaseResult
```

**Why the names are not HTTP names:** `SkuNotFound` rather than `NotFound404`. The repository
reports what it found in the database. The service turns that into a domain exception, and the

You've got the core idea: three outcomes, one sealed type, and that's why the service's `when` needs no `else`. One correction and then the parts you skipped.

**Correction: `SkuNotFound` and `InsufficientStock` aren't exceptions.** They're plain values that just report "here's what the SQL found". Nothing gets thrown in the repository. The service is the first place an exception appears. That split is deliberate:

```
repository   →  PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound      "no row"            (a fact)
service      →  throw SkuNotFoundException      "that's an error"   (a decision)
handler      →  404 text/plain                  "that's the HTTP"   (a translation)
```

For the same reason they're named `SkuNotFound`, not `NotFound404`. The repository doesn't know HTTP exists.

**`sealed` (#1), more precisely.** "Defines our types at compile time" is close. The exact rule: every implementation of `PurchaseResult` must live in the **same package and module**, so no other code can add a fourth case. Because the list is closed, the compiler can check that a `when` covers every case.

The real reason to skip the `else` is what happens later. Say a teammate adds a fourth case. Without an `else`, every `when` that doesn't handle it **stops compiling** and points at the exact line. With an `else`, the new case silently falls into whatever the `else` does. Leaving out `else` means the compiler finds every place that needs updating for you.

Java 17 has the same feature: `sealed interface PurchaseResult permits Purchased, SkuNotFound, InsufficientStock`.

**`data class` vs. `data object` (#2).** This comes down to whether a case **carries data**:
- `Purchased` carries the remaining `InventoryItem`, which is different for every purchase, so it needs a class with a constructor: `Purchased(item)`.
- The failures carry nothing, so one shared instance is enough. `object` declares the class and creates its single instance in one step (a singleton), which is why you write `PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound` with no `()`.
- The `data` on the object gives it a readable `toString()`: a failing test prints `expected: <InsufficientStock> but was: <SkuNotFound>` instead of `PurchaseResult$SkuNotFound@1b6d3586`.

**Nesting (#3).** Because the cases are declared inside the braces, their full names are `PurchaseResult.Purchased` and so on. That groups them under their parent, and the name `Purchased` can't clash with anything else. It's like a Java `static` nested class.

**Alternatives you rejected (#4).**
- **Throw from the repository**, the way `getInventory` throws when a SKU is missing? That works, but then the repository decides what counts as an error, and that's the service's job.
- **`InventoryItem?` and a second query** to find out why it was `null`? That opens a race: the stock could change between the two queries.
- **An `enum` plus a nullable item?** The compiler couldn't guarantee that `PURCHASED` always comes with an item.

---

3	package com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory
4	
5	import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient
6	import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository
7	
8	
9	/** Reads and writes inventory rows from Postgres, used by the service layer. */
10	@Repository
11	class InventoryRepository(
12	    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
13	){
14	    
15	    /** Returns every SKU with its quantity, sorted by SKU id; zero-stock SKUs included, empty list when none. */
16	    fun findAll(): List<InventoryItem> = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory ORDER BY sku_id")
17	    
18	    // Why: Chose the result set lambda instead of InventoryItem::class.java so Kotlin sees the items as non null.
19	            .query { rs, _ -> 
20	                InventoryItem(rs.getString("sku_id"), rs.getInt("quantity"))
21	            }
22	            .list()
23	            
24	            
25	    /** Returns a SKU with its quantity for a specific SKU. Will return null if no such SKU exists */        
26	    fun findBySkuId(skuId: String): InventoryItem? = jdbcClient.sql("SELECT sku_id, quantity FROM inventory WHERE sku_id = :skuId")
27	
28	    // Why: We parameterized the skuid instead of adding it directly to the sql above for sql injection prevention. 
29	            .param("skuId", skuId)
30	            .query{rs, _ ->
31	                InventoryItem(skuId = rs.getString("sku_id"), quantity = rs.getInt("quantity"))
32	            }
33	    // Why: The list singleOrNull below, we did this over the Java optional so we can stay within kotlin. We wont have more than one entry in the list because sku_id is the primary key so it is unique.
34	            .list().singleOrNull()
35	            
36	    
37	    /**
38	     * Adds quantity to a SKU's stock, creating the SKU if it doesn't exist yet, and returns the row with the new total.
39	     * Returns null, changing nothing, only if the new total would go past Int.MAX_VALUE. Quantity must be at least 1.
40	     */
41	    fun addStock(skuId: String, quantity: Int): InventoryItem? = jdbcClient.sql(
42	    // Why: one upsert instead of find-then-insert, so concurrent requests can't race each other.
43	    // Why: the overflow guard in the WHERE clause is written as current <= MAX - new, because current + new would itself overflow in Postgres.
44	        """ 
45	            INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity)  
46	                VALUES (:skuId, :quantity) 
47	                    ON CONFLICT (sku_id) 
48	                        DO UPDATE SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity

553	### The SQL: a data-modifying CTE
554	
555	```kotlin
556	"""
557	    WITH purchased AS (
558	        UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - :requested_quantity
559	            WHERE sku_id = :skuId AND quantity >= :requested_quantity
560	                RETURNING quantity
561	    )
562	    SELECT
563	        (SELECT quantity FROM purchased) AS remaining_quantity,
564	            EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM inventory WHERE sku_id = :skuId) AS sku_exists
565	"""
566	)
567	```
568	
569	This is the densest part of the project, so the SQL is explained one piece at a time.
570	
571	**SQL (`WITH ... AS (...)`, a CTE):** `WITH name AS (query)` defines a **common table expression**
572	(CTE): a named, temporary result that the rest of the statement can read like a table. It's
573	similar to declaring a local `val` and then using it below. Here the CTE is an `UPDATE`, not a
574	`SELECT`. Postgres calls that a **data-modifying CTE**. The `UPDATE` runs exactly once, and its
575	`RETURNING` rows become the contents of `purchased`.
576	
577	**SQL (the conditional `UPDATE`):**
578	
579	| Part | What it does |
580	| --- | --- |
581	| `SET quantity = quantity - :requested_quantity` | subtract the requested amount |
582	| `WHERE sku_id = :skuId` | only this SKU (an exact, case-sensitive match) |
583	| `AND quantity >= :requested_quantity` | only if there's enough. `>=`, not `>`, so selling the last unit is allowed |
584	| `RETURNING quantity` | send back the new quantity; if no row was updated, send back nothing |
585	
586	So `purchased` has **one row** (the remaining stock) if the purchase happened, and **no rows** if
587	it didn't. No rows can mean either "no such SKU" or "not enough stock". The outer `SELECT` tells
588	the two apart.
589	
590	**SQL (the outer `SELECT` has no `FROM`):** `SELECT a, b` without `FROM` returns exactly **one row**
591	built from the two expressions. That's always true, whatever the data. That's why the Kotlin below
592	can use `.single()`.
593	
594	**SQL (a scalar subquery):** `(SELECT quantity FROM purchased)` in parentheses, used as a value,
595	is a **scalar subquery**. It yields the single value if there's one row, and SQL `NULL` if there
596	are none. (Two rows would be an error, but the `WHERE sku_id =` on a primary key can't update two.)
597	So `remaining_quantity` is the new stock, or `NULL` for "nothing was bought".
598	
599	**SQL (`EXISTS` and `SELECT 1`):** `EXISTS (subquery)` is `true` if the subquery returns at least
600	one row, and `false` otherwise. It's never `NULL`. The `1` in `SELECT 1` is a placeholder: `EXISTS`
601	only checks whether a row comes back, not what's in it, so the convention is to select a constant.
602	`SELECT sku_id` would give the same answer.
603	
604	**SQL (`AS` names the columns):** `AS remaining_quantity` and `AS sku_exists` label the two result
605	columns. The Kotlin reads them by those names.
606	
607	**The trap: one snapshot for the whole statement.** Every part of one SQL statement reads the
608	database as it was when the statement *started*. The main `SELECT` does **not** see the `UPDATE`
609	made in the `WITH`, even though the `UPDATE` appears first. The only way to see the change is through
610	the CTE's `RETURNING`. Robert's first draft read the new quantity with `SELECT quantity FROM
611	inventory` in the outer query, and got the *old* stock back (5, not 3). Two consequences follow:
612	
613	- `remaining_quantity` must come from `purchased` (the `RETURNING` row), not from `inventory`.
614	- `EXISTS (... FROM inventory ...)` reading the old snapshot is **fine**: an `UPDATE` never adds or
615	  removes rows, so "does the row exist?" has the same answer before and after it.
616	
617	**Concurrency: why two buyers can't both get the last unit.** Postgres's default isolation level is
618	`READ COMMITTED`. When two statements try to update the same row, the second waits for the first
619	to commit or roll back. Then it **re-checks its `WHERE` clause against the newest version of that
620	row** before it writes. This is the one exception to "one snapshot for the whole statement": a row
621	the `UPDATE` finds already changed by a committed transaction is re-evaluated against its newest
622	version. The `EXISTS` and everything else in the statement still read the snapshot. With
623	`widget` at 1 and two purchases of 1:
624	
625	| Step | Purchase A | Purchase B | Row |
626	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
627	| 1 | `UPDATE` finds the row (1 ≥ 1), locks it, and writes 0 | | 0 (uncommitted) |
628	| 2 | | `UPDATE` finds the row, waits for A's lock | |
629	| 3 | commits → `remaining_quantity = 0` → `Purchased` | | 0 |
630	| 4 | | re-checks `0 >= 1`: false, updates nothing | 0 |
631	| 5 | | `remaining_quantity = NULL`, `sku_exists = true` → `InsufficientStock` | 0 |
632	
633	The check and the write happen together, on the latest committed value of the row. The
634	[same-SKU purchase race](../../test/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md#the-same-sku-purchase-race)
635	tests this with many threads, and the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint is the backstop if the
636	SQL were ever wrong.
637	
638	**Kotlin (raw string):** the SQL is a [raw string](#the-upsert). The deeper indentation on each
639	line is Robert's layout. Postgres ignores it.

644	.param("skuId", skuId)
645	.param("requested_quantity", quantity)
646	```

648	**Spring:** `:skuId` appears **twice** in the SQL (in the `UPDATE` and in the `EXISTS`), and one
649	`.param("skuId", ...)` fills both. Named parameters are matched by name, not by position. With JDBC's
650	positional `?`, the same value would have to be bound twice. The names are chosen by the author,
651	and each one only has to match its `.param` call. This file uses both `camelCase` (`:skuId`) and
652	`snake_case` (`:requested_quantity`), which is legal. `requested_quantity` makes it clear which
653	quantity is meant, since the table also has a `quantity` column.

655	### Reading the row: `NULL` is not `0`
656	
657	```kotlin
658	.query{rs, _ ->
659	        // Why: Used the javaObjectType so null stays null. JDBC getInt would turn null into 0, but 0 is a valid use case here. Meaning the last unit was just sold now the stock is 0. Null would be nothing was bought. We need to keep these distinct.
660	        val remainingQuantity: Int? = rs.getObject("remaining_quantity", Int::class.javaObjectType)
661	            val skuExists = rs.getBoolean("sku_exists")
662	```
663	
664	**JDBC (why not `getInt`):** `rs.getInt(...)` returns a Java primitive `int`, which can't hold
665	null, so JDBC returns **`0` for SQL `NULL`**. Here that would be a bug. `0` means "you just bought
666	the last unit" (a `Purchased`), and `NULL` means "nothing was bought". With `getInt`, a refused
667	purchase would look like a successful one that left 0 in stock. The repository test
668	`removeStock can sell the last unit and keeps the row at zero` depends on keeping the two apart.
669	(Java's other workaround is to call `getInt` and then `rs.wasNull()`.)
670	
671	**Kotlin (`Int::class.javaObjectType`):** JDBC's `getObject(column, Class<T>)` returns the value as
672	the requested Java class, or `null` for SQL `NULL`. The class has to be one that can hold `null`:
673	
674	| Kotlin expression | Java class | Can it be `null`? |
675	| --- | --- | --- |
676	| `Int::class.java` | `int.class` (primitive) | no |
677	| `Int::class.javaObjectType` | `Integer.class` (boxed) | yes |
678	
679	Kotlin has one `Int` type, and the compiler chooses between Java's `int` and `Integer` for you. When
680	a Java API asks for a `Class`, you have to choose: `.java` gives the primitive, `.javaObjectType`
681	gives the boxed class.
682	
683	**Kotlin (declaring `Int?`):** `getObject` is a Java method without nullability annotations, so its
684	result is a [platform type](../../build.gradle.kts.md#compiler-options), `Int!`, which Kotlin lets
685	you treat as either `Int` or `Int?`. Writing `: Int?` on the `val` is the important choice. With
686	`: Int`, the code would compile, and Kotlin would insert a null check that throws a
687	`NullPointerException` on every refused purchase. The type annotation turns a runtime crash into
688	something the compiler tracks.
689	
690	A correction, recorded honestly: while coaching, Claude first suggested `Integer::class.java`. In
691	Kotlin that refers to `java.lang.Integer` and gives the type `Integer!`, which the compiler
692	refused to assign to `Int?`. `Int::class.javaObjectType` is the idiomatic way to write it.
693	
694	**JDBC (`getBoolean` is safe):** `EXISTS` is always `true` or `false`, never `NULL`, so the primitive
695	`getBoolean` can't lose information here.
696	
697	**Kotlin (layout):** each line in the lambda is indented further than the one above it. That's only
698	layout: they're statements in sequence, not nested blocks. Only braces create nesting in Kotlin.
699	
700	### Choosing the outcome: a `when` without a subject
701	
702	```kotlin
703	            when {
704	                remainingQuantity != null -> PurchaseResult.Purchased(InventoryItem(skuId, remainingQuantity))
705	                skuExists -> PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock
706	                else -> PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound
707	            }
708	}
709	.single()
710	```
711	
712	**Kotlin (`when` without a subject):** `when { cond -> value ... }` with nothing after `when` is
713	an `if` / `else if` chain. Each branch is a boolean condition, they're checked **top to bottom**,
714	and the first true one wins. Java equivalent:
715	
716	```java
717	if (remainingQuantity != null) return new Purchased(new InventoryItem(skuId, remainingQuantity));
718	else if (skuExists) return InsufficientStock.INSTANCE;
719	else return SkuNotFound.INSTANCE;
720	```
721	
722	`else` is required here because the `when` is used as a value: the compiler can't prove that
723	arbitrary boolean conditions cover every case. (A `when` used only as a statement may leave `else` out.)
724	Compare this with the service's `when`, which checks the *type* of a sealed value and needs no
725	`else` (see [exhaustive `when`](InventoryService.kt.md#purchaseinventory-one-branch-per-outcome)).
726	
727	**Why the order matters:** a successful purchase *also* has `sku_exists = true`. If
728	`skuExists ->` came first, every successful purchase would be reported as `InsufficientStock`.
729	The branches go from most specific to least: "something was bought" → "the row exists, so there
730	wasn't enough" → "no row".
731	
732	| `remaining_quantity` | `sku_exists` | Result |
733	| --- | --- | --- |
734	| `3` (or `0`) | `true` | `Purchased(InventoryItem(skuId, 3))` |
735	| `NULL` | `true` | `InsufficientStock` |
736	| `NULL` | `false` | `SkuNotFound` |
737	
738	**Kotlin (smart cast):** `remainingQuantity` is `Int?`, but `InventoryItem`'s `quantity` is a
739	non-null `Int`. The branch compiles because once `remainingQuantity != null` is true, the compiler
740	treats `remainingQuantity` as `Int` inside that branch. That's a **smart cast**. It works because
741	`remainingQuantity` is a local variable that nothing can change between the check and the use, and
742	declaring it `val` guarantees that. (A property another thread could change wouldn't smart cast.)
743	Java has no equivalent; you'd use the value and trust that the check was right.
744	
745	**Kotlin (the lambda's value):** the lambda has two statements (`val`s) and then the `when`. As
746	with every lambda, the [last expression is the return value](#mapping-each-row-the-lambda), so
747	the `when`'s result, a `PurchaseResult`, is what the row mapper produces. The `when` is used as an
748	expression, not a statement, so each branch provides a value.
749	
750	**Why `skuId` and not a column:** `RETURNING quantity` doesn't return the SKU, so the item is
751	built from the function's `skuId` parameter. That's the same string, because the `WHERE` matched it
752	exactly.
753	
754	**Spring (`.single()`):** this is `JdbcClient`'s `single()`, not Kotlin's `List.single()`. It runs
755	the query and returns the one mapped row, and it throws if there are zero rows or more than one. Here
756	that can't happen, because the outer `SELECT` has no `FROM` and always returns exactly one row. That
757	guarantee is what makes `.single()` the correct choice here, where `addStock` needed
758	`.list().singleOrNull()`.

**SQL (a scalar subquery):** `(SELECT quantity FROM purchased)` in parentheses, used as a value,
is a **scalar subquery**. It yields the single value if there's one row, and SQL `NULL` if there
are none. (Two rows would be an error, but the `WHERE sku_id =` on a primary key can't update two.)
So `remaining_quantity` is the new stock, or `NULL` for "nothing was bought".

**SQL (`EXISTS` and `SELECT 1`):** `EXISTS (subquery)` is `true` if the subquery returns at least
one row, and `false` otherwise. It's never `NULL`. The `1` in `SELECT 1` is a placeholder: `EXISTS`
only checks whether a row comes back, not what's in it, so the convention is to select a constant.
`SELECT sku_id` would give the same answer.

**SQL (`AS` names the columns):** `AS remaining_quantity` and `AS sku_exists` label the two result
columns. The Kotlin reads them by those names.

**The trap: one snapshot for the whole statement.** Every part of one SQL statement reads the
database as it was when the statement *started*. The main `SELECT` does **not** see the `UPDATE`
made in the `WITH`, even though the `UPDATE` appears first. The only way to see the change is through
the CTE's `RETURNING`. Robert's first draft read the new quantity with `SELECT quantity FROM
inventory` in the outer query, and got the *old* stock back (5, not 3). Two consequences follow:

- `remaining_quantity` must come from `purchased` (the `RETURNING` row), not from `inventory`.
- `EXISTS (... FROM inventory ...)` reading the old snapshot is **fine**: an `UPDATE` never adds or
  removes rows, so "does the row exist?" has the same answer before and after it.

**Concurrency: why two buyers can't both get the last unit.** Postgres's default isolation level is
`READ COMMITTED`. When two statements try to update the same row, the second waits for the first
to commit or roll back. Then it **re-checks its `WHERE` clause against the newest version of that
row** before it writes. This is the one exception to "one snapshot for the whole statement": a row
the `UPDATE` finds already changed by a committed transaction is re-evaluated against its newest
version. The `EXISTS` and everything else in the statement still read the snapshot. With
`widget` at 1 and two purchases of 1:

| Step | Purchase A | Purchase B | Row |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `UPDATE` finds the row (1 ≥ 1), locks it, and writes 0 | | 0 (uncommitted) |
| 2 | | `UPDATE` finds the row, waits for A's lock | |
| 3 | commits → `remaining_quantity = 0` → `Purchased` | | 0 |
| 4 | | re-checks `0 >= 1`: false, updates nothing | 0 |
| 5 | | `remaining_quantity = NULL`, `sku_exists = true` → `InsufficientStock` | 0 |

The check and the write happen together, on the latest committed value of the row. The
[same-SKU purchase race](../../test/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md#the-same-sku-purchase-race)
tests this with many threads, and the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint is the backstop if the
SQL were ever wrong.

**Kotlin (raw string):** the SQL is a [raw string](#the-upsert). The deeper indentation on each
line is Robert's layout. Postgres ignores it.

### Binding the parameters

```kotlin
.param("skuId", skuId)
.param("requested_quantity", quantity)
```

**Spring:** `:skuId` appears **twice** in the SQL (in the `UPDATE` and in the `EXISTS`), and one
`.param("skuId", ...)` fills both. Named parameters are matched by name, not by position. With JDBC's
positional `?`, the same value would have to be bound twice. The names are chosen by the author,
and each one only has to match its `.param` call. This file uses both `camelCase` (`:skuId`) and
`snake_case` (`:requested_quantity`), which is legal. `requested_quantity` makes it clear which
quantity is meant, since the table also has a `quantity` column.

### Reading the row: `NULL` is not `0`

```kotlin
.query{rs, _ ->
        // Why: Used the javaObjectType so null stays null. JDBC getInt would turn null into 0, but 0 is a valid use case here. Meaning the last unit was just sold now the stock is 0. Null would be nothing was bought. We need to keep these distinct.
        val remainingQuantity: Int? = rs.getObject("remaining_quantity", Int::class.javaObjectType)
            val skuExists = rs.getBoolean("sku_exists")
```

**JDBC (why not `getInt`):** `rs.getInt(...)` returns a Java primitive `int`, which can't hold
null, so JDBC returns **`0` for SQL `NULL`**. Here that would be a bug. `0` means "you just bought
the last unit" (a `Purchased`), and `NULL` means "nothing was bought". With `getInt`, a refused
purchase would look like a successful one that left 0 in stock. The repository test
`removeStock can sell the last unit and keeps the row at zero` depends on keeping the two apart.
(Java's other workaround is to call `getInt` and then `rs.wasNull()`.)

**Kotlin (`Int::class.javaObjectType`):** JDBC's `getObject(column, Class<T>)` returns the value as
the requested Java class, or `null` for SQL `NULL`. The class has to be one that can hold `null`:

| Kotlin expression | Java class | Can it be `null`? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Int::class.java` | `int.class` (primitive) | no |
| `Int::class.javaObjectType` | `Integer.class` (boxed) | yes |

Kotlin has one `Int` type, and the compiler chooses between Java's `int` and `Integer` for you. When
a Java API asks for a `Class`, you have to choose: `.java` gives the primitive, `.javaObjectType`
gives the boxed class.

**Kotlin (declaring `Int?`):** `getObject` is a Java method without nullability annotations, so its
result is a [platform type](../../build.gradle.kts.md#compiler-options), `Int!`, which Kotlin lets
you treat as either `Int` or `Int?`. Writing `: Int?` on the `val` is the important choice. With
`: Int`, the code would compile, and Kotlin would insert a null check that throws a
`NullPointerException` on every refused purchase. The type annotation turns a runtime crash into
something the compiler tracks.

A correction, recorded honestly: while coaching, Claude first suggested `Integer::class.java`. In
Kotlin that refers to `java.lang.Integer` and gives the type `Integer!`, which the compiler
refused to assign to `Int?`. `Int::class.javaObjectType` is the idiomatic way to write it.

**JDBC (`getBoolean` is safe):** `EXISTS` is always `true` or `false`, never `NULL`, so the primitive
`getBoolean` can't lose information here.

**Kotlin (layout):** each line in the lambda is indented further than the one above it. That's only
layout: they're statements in sequence, not nested blocks. Only braces create nesting in Kotlin.

### Choosing the outcome: a `when` without a subject

```kotlin
            when {
                remainingQuantity != null -> PurchaseResult.Purchased(InventoryItem(skuId, remainingQuantity))
                skuExists -> PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock
                else -> PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound
            }
}
.single()
```

**Kotlin (`when` without a subject):** `when { cond -> value ... }` with nothing after `when` is
an `if` / `else if` chain. Each branch is a boolean condition, they're checked **top to bottom**,
and the first true one wins. Java equivalent:

```java
if (remainingQuantity != null) return new Purchased(new InventoryItem(skuId, remainingQuantity));
else if (skuExists) return InsufficientStock.INSTANCE;
else return SkuNotFound.INSTANCE;
```

`else` is required here because the `when` is used as a value: the compiler can't prove that
arbitrary boolean conditions cover every case. (A `when` used only as a statement may leave `else` out.)
Compare this with the service's `when`, which checks the *type* of a sealed value and needs no
`else` (see [exhaustive `when`](InventoryService.kt.md#purchaseinventory-one-branch-per-outcome)).

**Why the order matters:** a successful purchase *also* has `sku_exists = true`. If
`skuExists ->` came first, every successful purchase would be reported as `InsufficientStock`.
The branches go from most specific to least: "something was bought" → "the row exists, so there
wasn't enough" → "no row".

| `remaining_quantity` | `sku_exists` | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `3` (or `0`) | `true` | `Purchased(InventoryItem(skuId, 3))` |
| `NULL` | `true` | `InsufficientStock` |
| `NULL` | `false` | `SkuNotFound` |

**Kotlin (smart cast):** `remainingQuantity` is `Int?`, but `InventoryItem`'s `quantity` is a
non-null `Int`. The branch compiles because once `remainingQuantity != null` is true, the compiler
treats `remainingQuantity` as `Int` inside that branch. That's a **smart cast**. It works because
`remainingQuantity` is a local variable that nothing can change between the check and the use, and
declaring it `val` guarantees that. (A property another thread could change wouldn't smart cast.)
Java has no equivalent; you'd use the value and trust that the check was right.

**Kotlin (the lambda's value):** the lambda has two statements (`val`s) and then the `when`. As
with every lambda, the [last expression is the return value](#mapping-each-row-the-lambda), so
the `when`'s result, a `PurchaseResult`, is what the row mapper produces. The `when` is used as an
expression, not a statement, so each branch provides a value.

**Why `skuId` and not a column:** `RETURNING quantity` doesn't return the SKU, so the item is
built from the function's `skuId` parameter. That's the same string, because the `WHERE` matched it
exactly.

**Spring (`.single()`):** this is `JdbcClient`'s `single()`, not Kotlin's `List.single()`. It runs
the query and returns the one mapped row, and it throws if there are zero rows or more than one. Here
that can't happen, because the outer `SELECT` has no `FROM` and always returns exactly one row. That
guarantee is what makes `.single()` the correct choice here, where `addStock` needed
`.list().singleOrNull()`.

We check the database, update the quantity, and return the remaining stock all in one sql call. We do this to try and avoid a race condition. The sql call is more complicated than the previous one in the repository.

We then to make sure there is enough stock for this item. 
Finally for the first half of the sql call we return our resulting quantity to a custom made variable we called purchased.

You have the shape right: one statement, update plus return, and `sku_exists` as a true/false check. Four things to tighten. The first one matters most in an interview.

**1. The stock check happens *during* the update, not after it.** You described it as "update the quantity… then make sure there's enough stock." It's actually one step: `AND quantity >= :requested_quantity` sits in the `UPDATE`'s own `WHERE` clause. Postgres only writes a row that passes the check, so a row with too little stock is never touched. Check and write are **atomic**. That's the whole oversell protection, and the interview answer is: "the stock check is a condition on the write itself, so there's no gap between checking and writing."

**2. `purchased` isn't a variable; it's a CTE** (common table expression): a named, temporary *result table* that the rest of the statement can read. The closest Kotlin analogy is a local `val`. Because it holds the `UPDATE`'s `RETURNING` rows, it has:
- **one row** (the new quantity) if the purchase happened;
- **zero rows** if it didn't, whether the SKU is missing or the stock is too low.

That's why the second half exists: zero rows alone can't tell you *which* failure it was.

The second half:
- `(SELECT quantity FROM purchased)` in parentheses is a **scalar subquery**. It gives the one value, or SQL `NULL` if `purchased` is empty.
- `EXISTS (SELECT 1 …)` is true if any row comes back. The `1` is a placeholder, since `EXISTS` only cares whether a row exists, not what's in it.
- The outer `SELECT` has **no `FROM`**, so it always returns **exactly one row**. Remember that for the `.single()` later.

**3. The race, made concrete.** Note that the two-statement version *doesn't oversell*, because the conditional `UPDATE` still protects the stock. What it gets wrong is the **reason** it reports:

| Time | Request A: purchase `gadget` ×1 | Request B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `UPDATE … WHERE sku_id='gadget'` → 0 rows (doesn't exist) | |
| 2 | | `POST /inventory/gadget` creates it with 10 |
| 3 | `SELECT` "why?" → row exists → **InsufficientStock → 400** | |

The right answer was a 404, "SKU not found", but the client is told "not enough stock" for an item that now has 10. The classic race that *does* oversell is the other order: `SELECT` the stock, check it in Kotlin, then `UPDATE`. Two buyers both read 1, both decide it's fine, and both write. Our design avoids both problems.

**4. The bonus you skipped: one snapshot.** Every part of a single SQL statement sees the database **as it was when the statement started**. The outer `SELECT … FROM inventory` would **not** see the `UPDATE` above it. It would return the old stock (5, not 3), which is what happened in your first draft. The only way to see the new value is through `RETURNING` → `purchased`. The `EXISTS` reading the old snapshot is fine, because an `UPDATE` never adds or removes rows.

Good. The `javaObjectType` reasoning is exactly right, and so is the branch-by-branch logic. Here's what's missing.

**`.single()` is about rows, not outcomes.** You linked it to "only one of the three options is true", but those are two separate things:
- `.single()` works because the outer `SELECT` has **no `FROM`**, so SQL always returns **exactly one row**, whether the purchase worked or not. (This is `JdbcClient`'s `.single()`: it throws if there are 0 rows or more than 1.)
- The lambda then runs **once** on that one row, and the `when` picks one of the three outcomes from its two columns.

`findBySkuId` can't use `.single()`. A missing SKU there returns **zero rows**, and `.single()` would throw. So it uses `.list().singleOrNull()` to turn zero rows into `null`. Same idea for `addStock`: when the overflow guard refuses, zero rows come back.

**Why this `when` needs an `else` (#2).** The service's `when` checks the *type* of a sealed value, and the compiler knows every possible type. Here each branch is an arbitrary boolean expression. The compiler can't prove that `remainingQuantity != null` or `skuExists` covers every case, and because the `when` produces a value, every path must give one. So `else` is required. That's the if / else-if chain version of `when`.

**Two Kotlin details you used without naming:**
- **Smart cast again.** `remainingQuantity` is `Int?`, but `InventoryItem` needs a non-null `Int`. Inside the `!= null` branch, the compiler knows it can't be null and treats it as `Int`. That works because it's a local `val`, so nothing can change it between the check and the use.
- **The `: Int?` on the `val` matters.** `getObject` is a Java method, so Kotlin doesn't know whether it can return null (a "platform type"). If you had written `: Int`, it would compile, then throw a `NullPointerException` on every refused purchase. Writing `Int?` makes the compiler track the null for you.

**And the lambda's value:** the lambda has two `val` lines and then the `when`. The last expression in a lambda is its return value, so the `PurchaseResult` from the `when` is what the row mapper produces. No `return` needed.

content.text:
Yes: a `when` stops at the **first** true branch. There's no fall-through, unlike a Java `switch` without `break`. And yes, `skuExists` is true for every successful purchase, so all of them would return `InsufficientStock`, and the client would get a **`400 Insufficient inventory for widget`**.

It's actually worse than a wrong message. The `UPDATE` has **already run and committed**, so `widget` really went from 5 to 3. The client is told the purchase failed while the stock was taken. A retry would take 2 more. That's why branch order goes from most specific to least specific. The tests catch it: every happy-path purchase test would fail, for example [InventoryControllerTest.kt:284](src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt#L284).

## 5. The 400 path: `InsufficientInventoryException` and its handler

**Role:** when the service throws, Spring's `@RestControllerAdvice` catches the exception and turns it into the `text/plain` response. You've built this pattern twice already (for `SkuNotFound` and overflow), so we'll keep this short.

[InsufficientInventoryException.kt:5-6](src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/error/InsufficientInventoryException.kt#L5-L6)
```kotlin
/** Thrown by the service when removeStock reports insufficient stock for the purchase. Mapped to a 400 by InventoryExceptionHandler. */
class InsufficientInventoryException(skuId: String) : RuntimeException("Insufficient inventory for $skuId")
```

[InventoryExceptionHandler.kt:75-83](src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt#L75-L83)
```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}/purchase.post - when there is insufficient inventory for a purchase call we return 400 text/plain.

/** Returns a 400 text/plain response with the message from the exception: Insufficient inventory for <skuId> */
@ExceptionHandler(InsufficientInventoryException::class)
fun handleInsufficientInventory(ex: InsufficientInventoryException): ResponseEntity<String> =
    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        .body(ex.message ?: "Insufficient Inventory")
```

2. `ex.message ?: "Insufficient Inventory"`: your constructor always sets a message, so why does Kotlin make you handle `null`?

Good summary. Let me fill in all three.

**1. No `val`: close, but it's about "property or not", not about changing it.** Kotlin constructor parameters come in three kinds:

```kotlin
class A(skuId: String)       // plain parameter: only usable during construction
class B(val skuId: String)   // + a read-only property: a.skuId works later
class C(var skuId: String)   // + a mutable property: c.skuId = "x" works
```

Mutability is `val` vs. `var`. **No keyword at all** means it's not stored on the object. Here `skuId` is only needed once, to build the message string passed to `RuntimeException(...)`, so a plain parameter is enough. With `val`, the handler could read `ex.skuId`, which would be useful if it ever needed to build a JSON error body with the SKU as a separate field. Java equivalent of the plain version: a constructor argument that you pass to `super(...)` and never assign to a field.

**2. Right idea; here's where it comes from.** `message` is declared on Java's `Throwable`, and `new RuntimeException()` with no argument really does have a `null` message. So Kotlin types it `String?` for **every** exception. The compiler looks at the declared type on `Throwable`, not at what your subclass happens to pass. In practice your fallback string never runs; it's just there to satisfy the type.

**3. Good point, and there's a second half to it.** You're right that other callers (a batch job, a message consumer) should get a clear "this purchase failed" without knowing about HTTP. The other half is **where the HTTP mapping lives**:

- The repository speaks database (`PurchaseResult`).
- The service speaks business (`InsufficientInventoryException`), with no idea it's behind a web API.
- The handler speaks HTTP (400, `text/plain`), in **one place** for every controller.

If the controller built the 400 itself, every controller that purchases would repeat that logic, and the service would have to leak `PurchaseResult` upward. Exceptions also travel up by themselves: nothing in between has to check and pass them along. That's why the controller stays a one-liner, and why the purchase 404 needed **no new code**. It reuses `SkuNotFoundException` and its existing handler.
